analysis.one_liner: Taxes oil company windfall profits and uses the money to help low-income drivers pay for gasoline.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote in any committee and died at the end of the 109th Congress, with no cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have charged large integrated oil companies an extra tax equal to half the profit they make on every barrel of crude sold above $40 (adjusted for inflation), for three years. The money would have gone into a federal trust fund to pay for a new program giving low-income households $25 to $75 a month toward gasoline when pump prices spike, plus the existing home energy assistance program. It also would have given a $1,000 tax credit to anyone buying a car that gets 30 miles per gallon or better.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income households that drive long distances to work, school, or medical appointments would receive gasoline payments of at least $25 and up to $75 per month when gas prices in their state run more than 15% above January 2005 levels. Existing LIHEAP recipients would see the home energy program funded with dedicated oil-tax revenue. Buyers of fuel-efficient vehicles would get a $1,000 tax credit.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-income commuters facing high gas prices

how_it_helps.text: Creates a Low-Income Gasoline Assistance Program: eligible households (income at or below 150% of poverty or 60% of state median income, driving at least 30 miles a day to work, school, or medical care) could receive $25-$75 per month toward gasoline, for up to three months per application, whenever a state's gas price exceeds 115% of its January 2005 baseline [S2][S3].

Imposes a 50% excise tax on the windfall profit of integrated oil companies — profit on each barrel sold above an inflation-adjusted $40 base price — effective for crude removed after December 31, 2005 and expiring three years after enactment [S2][S3].

Routes the windfall tax revenue into a dedicated Energy Assistance Trust Fund for the gasoline program and the Low-Income Home Energy Assistance Act, and authorizes $500 million per year in appropriations for the gasoline program [S2][S3].
Provides a $1,000 tax credit for vehicles rated at 30 miles per gallon or better, available for tax years through 2008 [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Integrated oil companies, which would pay 50% of the profit on each barrel above an inflation-adjusted $40 base price. Companies could shrink the tax by investing in drilling, refineries, renewable fuel facilities, or biofuel plants, and the tax would be deductible against income tax. Some economists argue a windfall tax on domestic production can discourage drilling and marginally raise prices for consumers.

drawbacks.text: The windfall tax is sharply limited in practice: companies can offset it dollar-for-dollar with 'qualified investment' in drilling costs, refinery construction, renewable power facilities, and biofuel plants, and the tax paid is itself deductible from income taxes, so the actual revenue collected could be far less than the headline 50% rate suggests [S3].

The gasoline benefit is small and narrow — $25 to $75 per month, capped at three months per application, only when prices exceed a fixed trigger — and households must drive at least 30 miles a day to qualify, leaving out low-income people who cannot drive or drive less [S3].

Windfall profits taxes can discourage domestic oil production: the federal windfall profits tax of 1980 is widely blamed by economists for reducing U.S. drilling and increasing reliance on imports, and a similar effect could modestly raise prices for all consumers.

The $1,000 vehicle credit goes to buyers of new fuel-efficient cars, which skews the benefit toward households wealthy enough to buy a new vehicle rather than the low-income families the gasoline program targets.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offers real but modest help to a narrow group — low-income long-distance commuters — funded by a tax on oil profits that companies could substantially avoid through investments and deductions. Its drawbacks are the small benefit amounts, strict eligibility, and the risk that the windfall tax discourages domestic production. On balance it would shift money from a highly profitable industry to struggling households, though its design blunts both the cost to industry and the help to families.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to three House committees and two subcommittees, none of which ever took it up, and it died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Frank Pallone introduced the bill on December 6, 2005, during a period of sharply elevated gasoline and home heating prices following the 2005 hurricane season [S1][S2].
No other member of the House signed on as a cosponsor [S4].

The bill was referred to the Ways and Means, Energy and Commerce, and Education and the Workforce committees, and then in 2006 to subcommittees on Energy and Air Quality and on education, where no hearings, markups, or floor action followed [S1][S5].
The bill received no vote in either chamber before the 109th Congress ended on January 3, 2007 [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Integrated oil companies were better off because the bill died: they never faced the windfall profits tax. Low-income households struggling with gasoline costs received no new assistance.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil companies that avoided the tax

for.name: Rep. Frank Pallone Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and was its sole sponsor.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee with jurisdiction over the tax provisions (chaired by Rep. Bill Thomas, R-CA)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and never scheduled a markup or reported it out.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Air Quality
against.role: Energy and Commerce subcommittee (chaired by Rep. Joe Barton-era leadership structure)
against.what_they_did: Received a referral in January 2006 and took no further action on the bill.

against.name: Oil and gas industry
against.role: Major integrated oil companies and their trade associations
against.what_they_did: Opposed windfall profits tax proposals during the 2005-2006 energy price debate, arguing such taxes would reduce investment and production.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Democratic sponsor, zero cosponsors from either party, and died in committees controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill would have taxed 50% of their profit on every barrel sold above an inflation-adjusted $40 base price for three years, though they could offset much of it through investment in drilling, refineries, and biofuels. Their profits during the 2005 price spike came directly out of what consumers paid at the pump.

industries.industry: Auto retailers and fuel-efficient vehicle makers
industries.note: A $1,000 credit for cars rated at 30 mpg or better would have nudged buyers toward efficient vehicles, boosting sales for makers and dealers of those models.

industries.industry: State social service agencies and tribal organizations
industries.note: States and tribes would have received federal grants to run gasoline assistance programs, with up to 10% for administration.
